Case report 
The early clinical features of this case have al- 
ready been reported in detail [17]. In summary, 
this male patient, with an uneventful previous his- 
tory, developed at the age of 54 a syndrome of

continous muscle fiber activity with the clinical, 
electrophysiological and drug response features 
of SMS, initially associated with nystagmus, im- 
paired leftward gaze and bladder dysfunction. 
The associate signs spontaneously cleared within 
a few months, while muscle rigidity and spasms 
were markedly improved by chronic oral diaze- 
pare treatment (30 rag/day), which maintained a 
satisfactory functional condition over the follow- 
ing six years. At the beginning of October 1979 the 
patient suddenly experienced a transitory worsen- 
ing of muscle stiffness, followed by intermittent 
dysphagia, dysarthria and dyspnea. When the pa- 
tient was admitted again to our Institute, he no 
longer had rigidity and presented only facial 
weakness and slightly reduced thoracic expan- 
sion. The following day dyspnea worsened so that 
he was referred to the intensive care unit (ICU) 
and required tmcheostomy and assisted ventila- 
tion for 3 days. Respiratory failure resolved spon- 
taneously, but generalized weakness and fatiga- 
bility soon developed. When discharged from 
ICU he presented with blepharoptosis, and facio- 
pharyngeal, masseter and tongue weakness, 
which became worse with exercise, as well as 
waekness of neck and arm muscles. Intravenous 
neostigmine improved the weakness and edro- 
 9 phoninm chloride immediately resolved the mus- 
cular deficits. Needle EMG and motor and senso- 
ry nerve conduction velocity studies were normal, 
while a 3 Hz repetitive stimulation test of the me- 
dian nerve at the wrist demonstrated a 20% decre- 
ment of the M response at the 5th stimulus. Serum 
levels of sarcoplasmic enzymes were in the nor- 
mal range; deltoid muscle biopsy revealed scat- 
tered type I fiber hypotrophy with an isolated 
lymphohistiocytic infiltrate. Conventional chest 
x-rays did not reveal a mediastinal mass. At that 
time no other significant instrumental or laborato- 
ry alterations were found. MG was diagnosed and 
treated by oral pyridostygmine, which markedly 
improved the clinical cond ion. In 1985 a routine 
blood sample revealed altered liver function. A 
test for hepatitis antigens was negative; a liver bi- 
opsy demostrated the pathological features of 
chronic active hepatitis (CAH) [20]. In 1986 the 
patient presented a transitory worsening of spinal 
muscle fatigability. Computed tomography (CT) 
revealed a round, partially calcified mass in the 
anterior-superior mediastinum, suggestive of thy- 
morea. CT of the brain showed slight diffuse cere- 
bral atrophy. In the following months clinical and 
EKG signs of congestive heart failure developed, 
so that thoracic surgery for thymoma was con- 
traindicated. Between 1987 and 1988 the patient 
developed a depressive disorder with delusional 
features. Since steroid treatment seemed hazar- 
dous, azathioprine was administered for 3 
months, then stopped because of leukopenia,

which occured in spite of drug holidays. At the 
end of 1988 the patient suddenly died at home; 
autopsy could not be performed. 
Immunological investigations 
Serum and CSF samples were obtained under in- 
formed consent in 1986 and 1987, when the pa- 
tient was not on immunosuppressive treatment. 
Normal values are given in brackets. 
Total serum gamma globulins were consistently 
elevated to 31% (11-21 ). On immunonephelome- 
try, IgG content was 2030 mg/dl (639-1349), IgA 
339 mg/dl (70-312), C3 complement fraction 74

mg/dl (83-177). On agarose gel electrophoresis 
the increased gammagiobulin showed a polyclon- 
al pattern. Circulating immunocomplexes were 
detected ( + + +) on PEG immunoprecipitation. 
Determination of anti-nicotinic acetylcholine re- 
ceptor antibodies (AChR-Ab), using fetal calf 
muscle as the antigen source [4], gave a positive re- 
sult with a level of 20.42 pmol/ml (R. Mantegaz- 
za, Istituto Neurologico C. Best& Milano, person- 
al communication). Homogeneous-type anti-nuc- 
lear Ab, detected by indirect immunofluorescence 
on Hep-2 cells, were present with a titer of 1 + 320. 
Anti-ds-DNA Ab were also detected by indirect 
immunofluorescence on Crithidia luciliae cells 
with a titer of 1 +40; anti-mitochondrial Ab were 
also present (I + I0). ICA, on the contrary, were 
absent. 
Finally, circulating anti-skeletal muscle antibod- 
ies were demonstrated by indirect immunofluor- 
escence on normal cryostatic longitudinal section 
of normal human muscle 6 p. pick (E. Scarpini, 
Clinica Neurologica II, Universit~ di Milano, per- 
sonal communication). 
T-lymphocyte subsets typed by immunobeads 
technique (Bio-Rad) showed CD4 30% (45-65), 
CD8 65%(25-35), null cells and B lymphocytes 6% 
(10-15), CD4/CD8 ratio 0.47 (1.8-2). HLA haplo- 
type was A2~9; CW6,X; B12(44),13; DR7, X; 
~w2,x. On immunonephelometry the CSF albumin con- 
tent was 34.5 mg/di (10-30), IgG 4.6 mg/dl (1.4-4). 
Albumin serum/CSF ratio was 107(> 130). Link 
IgG index was 0.24(<0.70). Paired serum and 
CSF samples examined by thinqayer polyacryla- 
mide gel isoelectrofocusing showed identical IgG 
oligoclonal bands in both the serum and CSF at 
pH 8.4-9.5. 
Irnmunocytochemistry studies were performed 
on rat brain tissue by the method previously de- 
scribed by De Camilli et al [2]. Both serum and 
CSF of the patient contained IgG strongly react- 
ing against pyramidal neurons in the layer VI of 
the cerebral parietal cortex. Moderate levels of 
cytoplasmic immunoreactivity were also visible in

neurons of the thalamic reticularis nucleus and 
Bergmann glia cells of the cerebellum. None of 
the control sera from healthy individuals (n 8) and 
neurological patients (n 28) including patients 
with autoimmune MG (n 11) produced a similar 
distribution of the immnnoreactivity. The serum 
of the patient also produced intense immunos- 
raining of hepatocytes when tested on rat liver tis- 
sue (M. Solimena, Yale University, New Haven, 
CT., U.S.A., personal communication). 
Discussion 
The disorders of motor neurons manifested by hy- 
peractivity [23] are clinically heterogenous disor- 
ders which in many respects still lack a conclusive 
nosographic def'mition. A question may arise as to 
whether the syndrome of muscular hyperactivity 
first presented by our patient should be classified 
as SMS (Moersch-Woltmann syndrome) or as an 
(encephalo) myelophaty with rigidity, spasm or 
continuous motor unit activity. Clearly, muscle 
hyperactivity was the prominent feature of this 
case and differentiates it from the reported cases 
of SMS in which muscle hyperactivity is oversha- 
dowed by an encephalomyelopathic process [8, 9, 
21, 7, 15]. However, other cases reported as SMS 
might be considered a more benign variant of an 
inflammatory encephalomyelopathy of unknown 
origin [10, 12]. We also [13] observed two steroid- 
responsive SMS patients without DM. One of 
them showed a hypodense cerebral lesion on CT 
and oligoclonal CSF banding, while the other had 
only the typical features of the Moersch-Wolt- 
mann syndrome. Thus, a clearcut distinction be- 
tween the two disease entities appears difficult. At 
present, we think that the acronym "SMS" is a 
more comprehensive, though provisional, term 
for all patients with a prominent continuous mo- 
tor unit activity syndrome and electrophysiologi- 
cal and drug response feature denoting mainly a 
CNS dysfunction. 
Recent reports point to an association of SMS 
with type I DM and support an autoimmune 
etiology of SMS cases with anti-GAD activity [18, 
22]. Most of these patients also presented evi- 
dence of multiple autoimmune disease associa- 
tion, especially of the polyendocrine type. How- 
ever, in a more recently reported series [20], it has 
been shown that only 12 out of 22 SMS patients 
had anti-GAD activity and only 5 had type I DM. 
Moreover, none of the reported SMS patients 
with "inflammatory" features had DM. In the pa- 
tient reported here anti-GAD autoantibodies 
were likewise absent: only an aspecitie neuronal 
immunostalning was detected. Obviously, we 
shall take into account that time had elapsed from 
SMS manifestations, but it is noteworthy that the 
other two non-diabetic, steroid-responsive SMS 
patients we have observed [13] presented no anti- 
GAD immunoreactivity in the acute stage of 
SMS. Nevertheless, the clinical and laboratory 
features of the present case strongly suggest a 
multiple organ-directed dysimmune derangement 
which could have involved CNS, even though the 
diagnostic criteria for neither systemic lupus 
erythematosus [5] nor for other definite systemic 
autoimmune syndromes are fulfilled. It is remar- 
kable too that SMS was followed in this case by 
MG, a sure autoimmune disease with a quite low 
prevalence, and by CAH, a disease in which auto- 
immunity is thought to be involved. On the whole, 
the reported data suggest that an altered regula-

tion of the immune system might be involved in 
SMS susceptibility, althoug a specific pathogenet- 
ic role of anti-GAD or of other autoantibodies re- 
mains to be determined. 
Another interesting feature of this case is radio- 
logical evidence of thymoma, also consistent with 
the finding of circolating anti-skeletal muscle an- 
tibodies [3]. It is common in MG, but a thymoma 
and anti-AChR antibodies were also found in two 
non-myasthenic patients presenting with a neu- 
romuscular hyperactivity syndrome [6]. A clinical 
picture resembling that of the "jerking-SMS" was 
described in association with a lung cancer [16] 
and other patients with SMS-like features and 
malignancies have been reported [1, 11]. More- 
over, both of our steroid-responsive patients deve- 
loped malignant neoplasms (breast and colon ad- 
enocarcinoma) two years after the onset of SMS 
[141. 
In conclusion, the present case summarizes some 
definite features which may suggest a relationship 
between muscle hyperactivity syndromes, autoim- 
mune and paraneoplastic disorders. Further in- 
vestigations are needed to elucidate the nosogra- 
phic and pathogenetic definition of the unusual 
disease entities discussed.
